source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ad Romanos
ΑΡΕΘΑ ∆ΙΑΚΟΝΟΥ
Εἰ καί μοι λύχνον αἰῶνος ταχὺς ἔσβεσεν οἶτος λαμπάδος ἡμετέρης φέγγος
ἀμερσάμενος, ἀλλά γ' ἄρ' ἤρκεσε λύσσῃ ἑῆς κακότητος ὁ δαίμων πᾶσαν ἐμὴν τελέσαι
στυγναλέην βιοτήν· θῆκέ με χήρην ἐγγὺς ἀειρομένου μοι μαζοῦ, οὐδ' ἐπὶ τέκνον
ἴδον καλὸν ἀθυρόμενον, ἡδὺ τοκεῦσιν ἄγαλμα παραγκάς· τῷ γέ με πένθος ἄτλητον
μαλερῷ τηκεδόνος δάμασε πυρσῷ· τρεῖς πρὸς ἐείκοσ' ἐποιχομένην ἐνιαυτοὺς ἔσχεν
τύμβος ὅδε ξεινοδόκος γενέθλης ἡμετέρης· ἔνθ' ὕφηνον γενετῆρες ἅπασι γηραλέοι
θρῆνον τιλλόμενοι πολιὴν καὶ χορὸς εὐγενέων στενάχοντες ἀδελφῶν Ἄννης
μνώμενοι ἀσπασίως εἴδεος ἀγλαΐης.
thought_title: Anna's lament over her early death and mourning family
orientation: The work opens with a first-person epigram spoken by Anna (or a persona speaking as Anna), who laments that death cut short her life at twenty-three, leaving her widowed, childless, and mourned by her aged parents and noble brothers.
pass_a_gloss: Even if swift doom of life extinguished my lamp, taking away the light of my lamp, yet indeed the demon was content in the rage of his wickedness to make all my life gloomy; he made me a widow near my breast being lifted up, nor did I see a beautiful child playing at my breast, a sweet delight to parents in their arms; for this reason unbearable grief subdued me with the consuming fire of wasting; this tomb, host to strangers, received me as I was going through three and twenty years of my family; there my aged parents wove a lament for all, plucking their grey hair, and the chorus of noble brothers groaned, remembering Anna gladly for the splendor of her beauty.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'widow' for χήρην; 'widowed' is banned.
The source uses μαζοῦ twice, referring to the breast where a child would play; 'breast' is the literal body part and fits the intimate maternal image.
ξεινοδόκος literally means 'receiving strangers' or 'host to strangers'; keeping the compound sense preserves the epithet's force.
γενετῆρες is a poetic word for parents, literally 'begetters'; 'parents' is the natural English equivalent and matches the brief's description of Anna's aged parents.
Glossary gives 'noble' for εὐγενέων; the phrase describes Anna's brothers as well-born.

pass_b_english: Even if swift doom quenched the lamp of my life, robbing me of its light, still the demon, in the rage of his wickedness, had power enough to make my whole life gloomy. He made me a widow while a child was still being lifted to my breast, and I never saw a beautiful child playing before me, a sweet delight at parents' knees. So unbearable grief subdued me with the consuming firebrand of wasting. This tomb, host to strangers, received me from my family as I was completing twenty-three years. Here my aged parents wove their lament, tearing out their grey hair, and the chorus of noble brothers groaned, fondly remembering Anna's beauty and splendor.

problems.why: ξεινοδόκος means ‘foreign‑born’ or ‘of foreign origin’, not ‘host to strangers’.
problems.fix: This tomb, of foreign origin, received me...

problems.quote: a sweet delight held in the arms for its parents
problems.why: 'παραγκάς' means 'at the side, in the arms' — the child is the delight held in the parents' arms, not 'held in the arms for its parents'.
problems.fix: a sweet delight in the arms of its parents
problems.ruling: Greek: 'sweet image of a child at the side'; translation adds 'for its parents', which is not in the text.

edits.old: This tomb, host to strangers, received me
edits.new: This tomb, of foreign origin, received me

edits.old: a sweet delight held in the arms for its parents
edits.new: a sweet delight in the arms of its parents

fixed: ξεινοδόκος means 'foreign-born' or 'of foreign origin', not 'host to strangers'; edited.
παραγκάς means 'in the arms' — the child is the delight in the parents' arms; edited.

problems.quote: while my breast was still rising
problems.source_quote: θῆκέ με χήρην ἐγγὺς ἀειρομένου μοι μαζοῦ
problems.why: Greek mentions being made a widow, no reference to the breast.
ξεινοδόκος means 'receiving strangers/guests,' not 'of foreign origin'; the tomb is hospitable/hosting, not foreign.
problems.fix: This hospitable tomb received me as I approached my twenty-third year.
problems.ruling: ξεινοδόκος likely = ξενόδους ‘hospitable to strangers’, not ‘of foreign origin’, altering tomb’s description.

problems.quote: never saw a beautiful child playing at it, a sweet delight in the arms of its parents
problems.source_quote: οὐδ' ἐπὶ τέκνον ἴδον καλὸν ἀθυρόμενον
problems.why: Greek says ‘nor did I see a beautiful child sighing’, not a playing child or parental delight.
problems.fix: nor did I see a beautiful child sighing
problems.ruling: ἀθυρόμενον means 'sighing/grieving,' not 'playing'; 'sweet delight in arms' adds unsupported parental imagery.

problems.quote: wove their lament, tearing their grey hair
problems.why: Greek describes weeping tears, not weaving lament or tearing hair.
problems.ruling: τιλλόμενοι means 'tearing,' but 'wove their lament' invents weaving; 'weeping tears' misreads participles.
μνώμενοι means 'remembering/longing,' not 'groaned'; στενάχοντες is 'groaning,' but claim conflates verbs.

edits.old: He made me a widow while my breast was still rising, and I never saw a beautiful child playing at it, a sweet delight in the arms of its parents.
edits.new: He made me a widow, and I never saw a beautiful child sighing at my breast, a sweet delight in the arms of its parents.

edits.old: This tomb, of foreign origin, received me
Here my aged parents wove their lament, tearing their grey hair, and the chorus of noble brothers groaned, remembering Anna's beauty and splendor with longing.
edits.new: Here my aged parents wept tears, plucking their grey hair, and the chorus of noble brothers remembered Anna's beauty and splendor with longing.

fixed: The source θῆκέ με χήρην means 'he made me a widow'; the breast reference is in the following clause about the child, so the English was wrong to attach it to the widowhood.
ξεινοδόκος means 'receiving strangers/guests', so 'hospitable' is correct; 'of foreign origin' was a mistranslation.
The source says οὐδ' ἐπὶ τέκνον ἴδον καλὸν ἀθυρόμενον, 'nor did I see a beautiful child sighing'; the English 'playing' and 'a sweet delight in the arms of its parents' misread the Greek.
The source θρῆνον τιλλόμενοι means 'weeping tears, plucking their grey hair'; the English 'wove their lament, tearing their grey hair' was wrong.
The source μνώμενοι means 'remembering', not 'groaning'; the English 'groaned' was a mistranslation.

problems.why: ὕφηνον θρῆνον means 'wove a dirge/lament', not 'wept tears'. The weaving metaphor is lost.
problems.ruling: Greek ὕφηνον θρῆνον = ‘wove a lament’; rendered as “wept tears”, losing the weaving metaphor.

edits.old: Here my aged parents wept tears, plucking their grey hair
edits.new: Here my aged parents wove a dirge, plucking their grey hair

fixed: Changed 'wept tears' to 'wove a dirge' because the source ὕφηνον θρῆνον means 'wove a lament/dirge', not 'wept tears'.

problems.quote: the demon, in the rage of his wickedness
problems.why: Is 'demon' literal devil or personified Death? 'Wasting' unclear agent.
problems.fix: Clarify if 'demon' is Satan, disease, or death personified.

problems.why: 'Host to strangers' is odd metaphor; does tomb welcome all dead?
problems.fix: Explain metaphor: tomb receives all equally, or 'stranger' to her family.

edits.new: the consuming firebrand of a wasting disease

fixed: The demon is the source's δαίμων, a supernatural agent of evil; the English 'demon' is accurate and needs no change.
The tomb is ξεινοδόκος, 'host to strangers'; the English 'host to strangers' is a faithful rendering and needs no change.
The source τηκεδόνος means 'wasting' or 'consumption'; the English 'wasting' is accurate, but adding 'disease' clarifies the noun for modern readers without changing the meaning.

previous_english: Though swift doom quenched the lamp of my life, robbing my light of its brightness, the demon's rage and malice were still enough to make my whole life gloomy. He made me a widow, and I never saw a beautiful child sighing at my breast, a sweet delight in the arms of its parents. So unbearable grief subdued me with the fierce fire of wasting. This hospitable tomb received me as I approached my twenty-third year. Here my aged parents wove a dirge, plucking their grey hair, and the chorus of noble brothers remembered Anna's beauty and splendor with longing.
